extraction.name: Visual Genome
extraction.description: Despite progress in perceptual tasks such as image classification, computers still perform poorly on cognitive tasks such as image description and question answering. Cognition is core to tasks that involve not just recognizing, but reasoning about our visual world. However, models used to tackle the rich content in images for cognitive tasks are still being trained using the same datasets designed for perceptual tasks. To achieve success at cognitive tasks, models need to understand the interactions and relationships between objects in an image. In this paper, we present the Visual Genome dataset to enable the modeling of such relationships. We collect dense annotations of objects, attributes, and relationships within each image to learn these models. Specifically, our dataset contains over 100K images where each image has an average of 21 objects, 18 attributes, and 18 pairwise relationships between objects. We canonicalize the objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases in region descriptions and questions answer pairs to WordNet synsets. Together, these annotations represent the densest and largest dataset of image descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, and question answers.
extraction.creator: Ranjay Krishna, Yuke Zhu, Oliver Groth, Justin Johnson, Kenji Hata, Joshua Kravitz, Stephanie Chen, Yannis Kalantidis, Li-Jia Li, David A. Shamma, Michael S. Bemstein, Li Fei-Fei
extraction.citeAs: Krishna, R., Zhu, Y., Groth, O., Johnson, J., Hata, K., Kravitz, J., Chen, S., Kalantidis, Y., Li, L.-J., Shamma, D. A., Bernstein, M. S., & Fei-Fei, L. (2016). Visual Genome: Connecting Language and Vision Using Crowdsourced Dense Image Annotations. arXiv preprint arXiv:1602.07332.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Visual Genome was collected and verified entirely by crowd workers from Amazon Mechanical Turk. The pipeline involved multiple task stages for each component: region descriptions, objects, attributes, relationships, region graphs, scene graphs, and question-answer pairs. Strategies were deployed to ensure data accuracy and diversity.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The dataset uses 108,249 images from the intersection of the YFCC100M (Thomee et al., 2016) and MS-COCO (Lin et al., 2014). These images are real-world, non-iconic images that were uploaded onto Flickr by users.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The dataset was collected over the course of 6 months after 15 months of experimentation and iteration on the data representation. Specific start and end dates are not provided.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Objects, attributes, relationships, and noun phrases in region descriptions and question-answer pairs were canonicalized to WordNet synsets. Attributes were normalized based on morphology (stemming) and mapped to WordNet adjectives. Prepositions were ignored for relationships as they are not recognized by WordNet.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For attribute prediction experiments, attributes were lowercased, lemmatized, and excess whitespace was stripped. For region description generation, non-alphanumeric characters were removed, and text was lowercased and stripped of excess whitespace.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Dense annotations of objects, attributes, and relationships were collected. For region descriptions, workers drew three bounding boxes and wrote three descriptions for each region, repeated until 50 descriptions per image. Workers were encouraged to write diverse descriptions, enforced by BLEU score thresholds. Bounding boxes had to cover all mentioned objects. For objects, workers extracted objects from descriptions and grounded them with tight bounding boxes, satisfying 'coverage' and 'quality' requirements. Previously drawn boxes were suggested to build co-reference chains. For attributes and relationships, workers added attributes to objects or connected pairs of objects with relationships based on the description text. Scene graphs were created by combining all region graphs, merging co-referenced objects with bounding box overlap greater than 0.8, confirmed by workers. For question-answer pairs, workers wrote two types: freeform (8 pairs per image, covering at least three 'Ws') and region-based (based on selected regions). Rules included starting questions with 'seven Ws', avoiding ambiguous/speculative questions, and ensuring precision and uniqueness, making them clearly answerable from the image.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: All data underwent a verification stage to eliminate incorrectly labeled objects, attributes, relationships, and vague/subjective/opinionated region descriptions and QAs. Verification used two strategies: majority voting and rapid judgments. All components except objects were verified by majority voting, where at least two out of three unique workers had to confirm correctness. Objects were verified using rapid judgments, an interface inspired by rapid serial visual processing, for increased speed.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Each image has an average of 21 objects, 21 attributes, 19 relationships, 42 region descriptions, and 17 question-answer pairs.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 33,000 unique workers contributed. 93.02% of workers were from the United States, with smaller percentages from the Philippines (1.29%), Kenya (1.13%), India (0.94%), Russia (0.50%), Canada (0.47%), and others (2.65%). The majority of workers were between 25 and 34 years old, with ages ranging from 18 to 68. There was a near-balanced split of 54.15% male and 45.85% female workers.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford's dependency parser (Manning et al., 2014) was used to automatically extract nouns as suggestions for object extraction. Word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013) was used to convert words in descriptions to 300-dimensional vectors for semantic analysis. Stanford NLP tools (Manning et al., 2014) were used to extract noun phrases for canonicalization.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset is described as an 'ongoing effort of collecting this dataset', implying continuous maintenance. However, specific versioning information, update timeframes, or deprecation policies are not detailed.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset aims to enable important applications such as image search, question answering, and robotic interactions by fostering a deeper, cognitive understanding of visual scenes. It is designed as a general-purpose representation of the visual world, without bias toward a particular task, for training and benchmarking the next generation of computer vision models. It is expected to help models develop a broader understanding of the visual world, complementing object detection with abilities to describe objects and explain their interactions and relationships.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is somewhat biased towards images of people. Certain sports (skiing, surfboarding) are overrepresented due to an image source bias. The distributions of relationships follow a Zipf distribution.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The canonicalization mappings are not perfect and still contain some ambiguity. Current models are unable to reason about complex images, as indicated by objectively low accuracy in region description generation. Models struggle to distinguish between different objects when not clearly visible or when abstract outlines are present. 'Where' and 'why' questions, involving spatial and common sense reasoning, tend to have more diverse answers and perform poorly in baseline QA tasks.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training and benchmarking next-generation computer models for comprehensive scene understanding, including cognitive tasks like image description and question answering. Specific applications include dense image captioning, visual question answering, image understanding (using scene graphs as evaluation metrics), relationship extraction, and semantic image retrieval. It can be used to develop NLP and vision models that can answer questions from descriptions, images, or both, and to improve semantic image retrieval and image captioning.
